abstract: Firms’ access to external finance differs widely across Europe. This column uses data from the ECB’s Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises to map these differences and to study what they mean for monetary policy. The authors find that countries in which firms face tighter financial frictions respond less to the ECB’s monetary policy changes, and that they face a worse trade-off between output and inflation. A model of the monetary union suggests that financial integration in the spirit of the Savings and Investments Union would make monetary policy more effective, but potentially at a cost to financial stability.
title: The geography of financial frictions

abstract: Raising educational attainment is the canonical way skills keep pace with technology. This column argues that changes in learning content matter just as much, drawing on five decades of legally binding German vocational training curricula linked to patents and administrative worker records. Occupational curricula more exposed to digital technologies are rewritten faster, mainly by adding new skills rather than discarding old ones. Entrants trained under the new content earn higher wages; older incumbents, who had completed the older curricula, see their wages fall.
authors: Anna Salomons, Cäcilia vom Baur, Ulrich Zierahn-Weilage
title: Updating what workers learn: Technology, training content, and the supply of expertise

abstract: Thermal power enterprises are major participants in China's carbon market and are central to the large-scale deployment of Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS). This study develops a three-player dynamic evolutionary game involving the government, financial institutions, and thermal power enterprises to examine how coordinated environmental policies drive CCUS technology diffusion across the initial, transition, and mature stages of technological development. We compare three policy instruments-carbon price, green credit, and government penalties and examine how their effects on enterprises' CCUS investment decisions vary across technological stages. The results show that in the initial stage, none of the three instruments is sufficient to alter enterprises' investment strategies. In the transition stage, the effect of carbon price becomes stronger, while green credit begins to influence investment decisions. In the mature stage, carbon price plays a more prominent role in supporting CCUS investment, green credit provides financing support, and government penalties strengthen regulatory incentives. Further analysis shows that policy coordination exhibits clear stage-dependent characteristics: its effect is limited in the initial stage, most pronounced in the transition stage, and mainly accelerates convergence toward CCUS investment in the mature stage. The introduction of government penalties further strengthens this convergence effect. Furthermore, higher capture efficiency improves CCUS investment profitability under the benchmark conditions, although the negative marginal effects of initial investment and unit capture costs do not necessarily weaken. Maintaining an appropriate CO2 utilization revenue-sharing ratio between financial institutions and thermal power enterprises is particularly important during the transition stage for balancing the interests of both parties and sustaining cooperation.

title: Stage-dependent policy coordination and CCUS technology diffusion in China's thermal power enterprises: A three-player dynamic evolutionary game

abstract: Do incidental emotional shocks affect political attitudes toward state authority? We link Chinese Super League football results to respondents’ interview dates in the Chinese General Social Survey (2015, 2018, 2021, and 2023) and exploit within-province-year variation in exposure to unexpected match outcomes, classified against pre-match betting odds. Upset losses by a respondent’s provincial team increase expressed acceptance of government intervention against public criticism; the effect fades over the week after the match. The response is most pronounced in attitudes toward public criticism: parallel items on government interference in private life, social trust, and happiness show no comparable movement. These findings are consistent with transient negative emotions increasing acceptance of government control over public criticism, a reversal of the same-valence pattern documented in the political-spillover literature.
